1: Let the superior take the credit in public; make them look capable, not diminished.
Display competence where the record will hold it, not in the superior's presence.
Pick the room and the moment; brilliance shown to the wrong person becomes a threat.
If talent outshines the boss, the cost falls on you, not on them.
2: Treat affection as no guarantee; rely on obligation, which has to be demonstrated.
Listen hardest to critics, who have a motive to tell you what actually happened.
An opponent who switches sides has to earn your trust, and the debt then expires.
Do not confuse approval with alliance; popularity is not a security arrangement.
3: Say nothing that lets others name your objective before you have committed.
Separate intent from action so commitment arrives as surprise, not confirmation.
Conceal the destination from rivals, but never the objective from your own people.
Readable intent gives opponents time to fortify, recruit allies and negotiate.
4: Every extra sentence widens the record that can be quoted, analysed or regretted.
Answer the narrow answerable question first, then stop while you still hold the room.
Finishing early leaves others to speculate, and speculation is not yours to correct.
Decide in advance what is worth having repeated before the questioning begins.
5: Power is granted by the judgement of others, and that judgement admits no appeal.
Reputation is built from small confirmations and lost to the one that contradicts them.
Treat character as a public asset to be managed, not a private fact you assume.
People who cannot verify your intentions substitute a prediction, and that is your standing.
6: Decisions go to people who know you exist; the unknown candidate is not a candidate.
Attention feeds on itself, since a crowd is read as proof of whatever it watches.
Send the story ahead of yourself so the audience arrives already persuaded.
Visibility is a two-way dependency; notice brings people who want something from you.
7: Delegate execution and keep the representing; the operator is paid for judgement.
Do the task yourself and you stay replaceable the moment it is finished.
Expect resentment from undercredited people; it surfaces later through other mouths.
If you take the credit, you can no longer inspect the work yourself.
8: Whoever must travel or wait is already subordinate during the interval.
Show that something is available, so the obligation to approach reverses.
Eagerness is disclosure; a visible need tells the room what can be extracted.
Bait only what you can deliver, since a broken promise costs you the next attempt.
9: Deliver a result that makes the argument obsolete; opinions do not settle contests.
Argue only where the listeners are the people who actually decide.
Defending a claim hard turns it into identity, and the exchange moves by counter.
Refusing to explain can easily be read as refusing to account for anything.
10: Choose your company deliberately, since association is an unauditable credit rating.
The circle around a leader exists partly to filter what reaches him and when.
Failing publicly rewrites your reputation for failure regardless of the real cause.
Expectation is contagious, so years among the aggrieved narrow your own range.
11: Control the only route to something necessary and arguments become unnecessary.
Indispensability is about presence at every decision point, not about legal power.
Never be one of two sources where a single route would do the same work.
A single point of dependency is a single point of failure; keep a substitute possible.
12: A concession that cannot be returned leaves the recipient unable to attack the giver.
Total war invites unlimited spending; mix part truth with a concession timed to land.
Generosity disarms only while it stays rare and its motive stays unexplained.
Severity shown repeatedly teaches everyone the price of attacking you.
13: Frame every request around what the other party gains from granting it.
Appeals to mercy or to past favour produce embarrassment and a quiet refusal.
Do the financial work an institution cannot, and the influence follows the service.
Give people something worth backing for its own sake, not only for what you gain.
14: Open inquiry makes you an enemy, so place yourself where news forms first.
Draw your sources from merchants, clerks, servants and listeners, not from officials.
Anyone telling you more than they appear to know is usually reporting upward.
Covert watching corrodes the trust it exploits; save it for what cannot be learned openly.
15: A rival who survives still holds men, money and the choice of ground and hour.
Every reprieve you grant is time handed to the other side to rebuild itself.
Mercy toward someone able to strike back defers the cost of the fight by a decade.
Check before the verdict, not after, whether the loser is genuinely finished.
16: Value rises as availability falls; constant presence turns a person into furniture.
Make access scarce, so the reward for service becomes a moment of your presence.
Ration your appearances rather than withdrawing entirely; reliability still matters.
The imagination fills an absence with something worse than the truth.
17: Keep your reactions unreadable so nobody can calculate how to provoke you.
Predictability is a flaw once observed; people arrange themselves around your pattern.
Terror applied evenly breeds the conspiracies it was meant to prevent.
Prefer fixed rules applied without favour over a temperamental mood.
18: A wall keeps out the enemy and also the people who report on the enemy.
Isolation turns a visible threat into an invisible one, and power dissolves inside it.
Security that depends on being unreachable is only as good as the last forecast.
Be difficult to reach, never difficult to attack, and stay in the flow of events.
19: Judge the person in front of you: some forget slights and some never do.
Spend outrage only where it produces advantage, not merely where it feels good.
Take the substance of a dispute and leave the grievance unexpressed.
Refusing to offend ever is its own failure, since no one then fears your office.
20: Never place your whole income, reputation or future inside one relationship.
Be useful to several centres at once, and owe each only what is presently owed.
Talleyrand outlived four regimes by being indispensable rather than loyal.
Withhold the whole fortune, but never withhold visible loyalty; suspicion ends careers.
21: Undersell your sharpness so opponents arrange their defence around the wrong version.
Appearing ordinary means nobody prepares for the second set of hands.
Understatement is a discipline about what others believe you are capable of.
If the private competence is thin, the disguise removes your last warning.
22: Give away everything so the winner's guard drops at the moment of celebration.
Strength spent finishing a surrendered opponent buys only the opponent.
Keep something in reserve, because a real capitulation leaves nothing to play.
A surrender that buys nothing surrenders everything, including your own safety.
23: Force committed in one direction is worth several times the same force spread thin.
Equal subdivision of your strength guarantees every part will be beaten in detail.
Hold a reserve outside the plan so one defeat cannot sever a single line.
Having more men than the enemy counts for nothing until they stand in one place.
24: Make your superior the source of every good idea and the only credible centre.
Manufacture each advance rather than announcing it, and absorb slights unwounded.
At court the decoration of a suggestion matters more than the suggestion itself.
Keep one competence strictly private; applause in the room is not access to the decision.
25: Treat your own past as negotiable; identity is a position, not an inheritance.
Build the new role before the old one fails under a world that has changed.
Keep one reserve of self that no audience is permitted to inspect.
A reinvention without substance is a costume, and costumes are read at the first test.
26: Keep your signature off the mechanism; personal blame is the one thing you cannot delegate.
Every intermediary is a witness, and the witnesses accumulate over time.
Deniability buys distance in time; it is a delay, not a permanent shield.
The moment your name attaches to an ugly act, the authority behind your orders is gone.
27: People organise around belonging rather than around agreeing with your argument.
Name what the group longs for, and give it a story large enough to live inside.
A promise that can never be tested becomes an argument for continuing to fund it.
Give followers a belief they can hold without depending on you personally.
28: Hesitation is legible as fear, and fear can be priced, outmanoeuvred and waited out.
Fix the hour and the ground rather than the bravado; entry itself must be decisive.
A man who has shown he will hesitate never fully regains being believed.
Make the first move irreversible only while it is still reversible.
29: Most plans are lost at the transition where the original one is exhausted.
Decide in advance who bears the blame and how failure will be announced.
Plan winter, distance and the day after victory, not only the opening move.
Name in advance who may abandon the plan, and at what point.
30: Visible strain invites others to estimate your ceiling and treat it as fixed.
Keep the labour private; advertisement of effort is a form of confession.
Move effort out of the public frame rather than staging ease you do not possess.
Delegate the visible strain to people whose dignity is not being spent.
31: Whoever fixes the range of available choices has already decided the outcome.
Propose a narrow decision, then narrow it further with apparent concessions.
Energy spent arguing what is possible is energy not spent on who chose it.
Leave the opponent one dignified route out, and make that route public.
32: People will prefer a flattering fiction to a modest truth about themselves.
Supply the story and you never have to persuade anyone of anything.
Fantasy is borrowed credit that must be renewed and always costs somebody else.
A public fantasy cannot survive a private audit; correct the record early.
33: Find the constraint a person cannot name, since a negotiation without it is at his mercy.
Listen for what people say rather than what they would be willing to write down.
Use what you know to create room to move, not to demonstrate that you know it.
Every thumb you press becomes a file, and the archive turns on its own keeper.
34: Most people cannot read merit but they can read manner, so manner sets the rank.
Dress, posture and distance confer authority in advance of any achievement.
Keep the public manner exact and the private manner available for honest advice.
Ceremony without substance reads as evidence, and audiences are good auditors of it.
35: A move made late reads as explanation; the same move made early reads as opinion.
Wait until the situation has resolved enough that your intervention seems inevitable.
Choose the moment rather than hesitating; a man waiting for certainty waits too long.
Time the arrival and have something true to say on the far side of it.
36: The sting of a refusal is the visible wish for the thing, not the refusal itself.
Do not explain your worth to the man who refused you; he is learning your price.
Pleading for an audience advertises the size of the prize to everyone else.
Reserve contempt for small things and argue hard for material ones.
37: Images arrive already interpreted; words can be quoted and turned back on you.
Stage the arresting picture rather than explaining yourself and becoming defensive.
If the imagery outruns the substance, the audience reads the gap as a lie.
Keep one anchor of plainness, so the spectacle reads as character and not ambition.
38: Keep convictions private and wear the room's manners; visible difference reads as contempt.
Blend into the crowd, because unorthodox conduct invites quiet punishment.
Conformity buys you the room in which an unorthodox idea can be planted.
A lifetime of performing the common touch leaves you unsure which self is yours.
39: Stay composed while the other side is forced to decide at the wrong moment.
Provoke a rival into revealing a plan or boasting; anger is their error, not yours.
Let the treachery mature instead of answering it on the day you discover it.
Manufactured rage appears on cue, and the room quickly learns to discount it.
40: Anything offered for nothing is either a trick or a debt, and both of them bind you.
Pay full price, so no one is owed anything and nothing is held as a favour.
Idle money is wasted money; circulate it for standing rather than for gratitude.
Price everything, including your own time, and keep the ledger visible.
41: A successor who competes on the predecessor's ground will be found wanting.
Change the terms of the contest rather than trying to outdo a legend.
Symbolism tells an audience in a moment which of two stories it is living.
Some forms of authority can only be carried; know which parts of precedent are load-bearing.
42: Most group disorder is organised and voiced by somebody who profits from it.
Remove the instigator and the followers find they have no argument of their own.
Do not negotiate with a dissenter who has only a use for grievance.
Make the removal read as order rather than persecution, or you build a martyr.
43: Force buys compliance and rents it dearly, because it manufactures the next crisis.
Learn what each person fears, wants and loves before you make any proposal.
Return a defeated leader to his community; killing him only produces a successor.
Attention is a form of power, and inattention means you have not met them at all.
44: Repeat their words, methods and values back until they must answer themselves.
Argument is the weakest instrument here, since the truth is resented more often than heard.
Being exactly understood is nearly impossible for a prospective ally to refuse.
Mirror enemies occasionally; mirroring the people you want to keep reads as mockery.
45: Everyone endorses change in the abstract and resists it on a given Tuesday.
Keep the forms people recognise, and change what sits behind them.
A population told for years that it is being improved will resist on principle.
Name the destination plainly; a settlement nobody sees as new will be defended by nobody.
46: Flawless superiority breeds envy in the group best placed to act on it.
Envy goes underground and returns as criticism, rumour and quiet sabotage.
Show an ordinary fault, or attribute the important part of the success to luck.
A person others can measure is safer than one they find impossible to measure.
47: Define the mark before you begin, and stop the moment it is reached.
Momentum gets mistaken for destiny, and each extra claim drains limited reserves.
The rare quality is the withdrawal rather than the advance.
Write the mark down beforehand, since it is hard to see from inside the moment.
48: Any plan with a visible shape can be studied, anticipated and struck in advance.
Refuse to hold one fixed posture, so the other side reveals his intention hunting yours.
A strategy practised until it is a habit has become the fixed shape to avoid.
Stay fluid while weaker, take shape to concentrate a strike, then disperse at once.
